clinicalPearls: More than 70% of U.S. adults are overweight or have obesity, and prevalence is rising in most industrialized nations, with accelerating rates in children and adolescents.

BMI (weight in kg divided by height in m squared, or weight in lb divided by height in in squared times 703) is used to classify weight status: healthy weight 18.5-24.9, overweight 25.0-29.9, obesity class I 30.0-34.9, class II 35.0-39.9, and extreme/class III obesity 40 or greater.

BMI only reflects body size; it does not capture body composition, fat distribution, or individual health, so it functions as a screening and population tool rather than a direct measure of adiposity.

Waist circumference is a surrogate for visceral adipose tissue and independently predicts metabolic syndrome, diabetes, and cardiovascular disease; it should be measured in the horizontal plane above the iliac crest, particularly when BMI is 35 or below.

Ethnic-specific waist cutpoints differ: for Europeans, greater than 94 cm in men and greater than 80 cm in women; for South Asians and Chinese, greater than 90 cm in men and greater than 80 cm in women.
Lower BMI thresholds for overweight and obesity have been proposed for the Asia-Pacific population because metabolic risk appears at lower body weights.

The obesity-focused history is best approached using neutral language (weight, excess weight, BMI, unhealthy weight) because terms like obesity, morbid obesity, or fatness are perceived as stigmatizing.

Recommended baseline workup for all patients includes a fasting lipid profile (total, LDL, and HDL cholesterol plus triglycerides), a chemistry panel, glycated hemoglobin, and blood pressure measurement.
Physical fitness and sedentary behavior are independent predictors of all-cause mortality regardless of BMI or body composition, underscoring the importance of an activity history.

Staging tools such as the AACE/ACE complication-based system (stage 0 with no complications, stages 1-2 with mild-moderate or severe complications) and the Edmonton Obesity Staging System (graded 0-4 across medical, functional, and psychological domains, independent of BMI) help identify high-risk patients beyond BMI alone.
As BMI rises by 5 kg/m2, cancer mortality is estimated to increase by about 10%, and obesity has reportedly overtaken smoking as the leading risk factor for cancer in some countries.
Not every patient meeting a BMI obesity threshold requires treatment, but those with obesity-related complications and comorbidities should be managed proactively.
harrison.pathophysiology: Obesity arises from a chronic imbalance in which energy intake exceeds energy expenditure, leading to expansion of adipose depots. It is a highly heterogeneous condition strongly influenced by underlying genetic variation, with environmental factors ubiquitous in developed and developing countries; in some individuals it is attributable entirely to genetic causes. Insulin resistance is one of the earliest complications: muscle (glucose disposal) and liver (glucose production) become less responsive to insulin, prompting compensatory hyperinsulinemia. Two main hypotheses link adiposity to insulin resistance—macrophage- and inflammatory-cell products in obese adipose tissue disturbing insulin action, and the limited storage capacity of adipose tissue causing ectopic lipid deposition in muscle and liver (human data are stronger for the ectopic-fat mechanism). The metabolic, endocrine, and cardiovascular consequences may stem from chronic overnutrition and ectopic fat rather than fat mass per se, whereas certain complications (osteoarthritis, reflux esophagitis, obstructive sleep apnea) relate more directly to mass and volume effects.
additionalDifferentials: Monogenic/syndromic obesity (e.g., Bardet-Biedl syndrome, POMC, PCSK1, or leptin receptor deficiency)
nonInfectiousMimics: Drug-induced weight gain (diabetes agents such as insulin, sulfonylureas, thiazolidinediones; steroid hormones; antipsychotics such as clozapine, olanzapine, risperidone; lithium; tricyclic antidepressants, MAO inhibitors, paroxetine, mirtazapine; antiepileptics such as valproate, gabapentin, carbamazepine)
Peripheral edema mimicking fat gain (NSAIDs, calcium channel blockers do not increase body fat)
additionalInvestigations: Fasting lipid profile (total, LDL, HDL cholesterol, triglycerides)
Glycated hemoglobin and chemistry panel for diabetes and metabolic screening
Waist circumference / waist-to-hip ratio for visceral adiposity
Targeted endocrine workup (thyroid, cortisol/Cushing evaluation) when secondary obesity is suspected
Sleep evaluation for obstructive sleep apnea when symptoms or risk factors present
redFlags: Features suggesting a secondary cause (e.g., signs of Cushing's syndrome, hypothyroidism, hypothalamic disease) warranting further evaluation
Severe hypertriglyceridemia sufficient to risk pancreatitis
Symptoms of obstructive sleep apnea or hypoventilation (heavy snoring, daytime somnolence, dyspnea)
Idiopathic intracranial hypertension presentation in a patient with obesity
Rapidly progressive metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease/NASH with signs of fibrosis or cirrhosis
harrison.prognosis: Obesity is a serious chronic disease associated with increased morbidity and mortality through multiple complications—type 2 diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidemia, atherothrombotic cardiovascular disease, stroke, heart failure (often diastolic dysfunction) and atrial fibrillation, obstructive sleep apnea, fatty liver disease that can progress to NASH and cirrhosis, several cancers, osteoarthritis, and gout. Risk generally rises with increasing levels of obesity and with central (visceral) fat distribution. Obesity also worsens outcomes from some infections (notably COVID-19) and raises susceptibility to wound infection and postoperative sepsis. Realistic initial treatment goals (around 8-10% weight loss over 6 months) can meaningfully improve obesity-related complications and quality of life.
pitfalls: Relying on BMI alone, which does not measure body composition or fat distribution and can misclassify individual risk.
Using stigmatizing language (obesity, morbid obesity, fatness) that leaves patients feeling judged and can undermine engagement.
Overlooking secondary or drug-induced causes of weight gain before attributing obesity solely to lifestyle.
Initiating lifestyle change when the patient is not ready, which can cause frustration and hamper future efforts.
Assuming all patients with a BMI in the obesity range require treatment, when BMI is an imperfect measure of disease.
Neglecting waist circumference, which adds independent risk information about visceral adiposity.
harrison.severityClassification: WHO/BMI classification: underweight under 18.5; healthy weight 18.5-24.9; overweight 25.0-29.9 (increased disease risk); obesity class I 30.0-34.9 (high risk); class II 35.0-39.9 (very high risk); class III/extreme obesity 40 or greater (extremely high risk). Complication-based staging (AACE/ACE): stage 0 no complications, stage 1 one or more mild-moderate complications, stage 2 at least one severe complication. The Edmonton Obesity Staging System grades 0-4 across medical, functional, and psychological domains independent of BMI.
management: Structured lifestyle intervention as the foundation: reduced-energy dietary plan, increased physical activity and behavioural/psychological support
Pharmacotherapy as an adjunct when lifestyle change is insufficient: GLP-1 (and dual GIP/GLP-1) receptor agonists, or orlistat, naltrexone-bupropion or phentermine-topiramate
Bariatric/metabolic surgery (sleeve gastrectomy or Roux-en-Y gastric bypass) for severe obesity or obesity with significant comorbidity
Screen for and treat obesity-related comorbidity: type 2 diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidaemia, obstructive sleep apnoea and fatty liver disease
Evaluate and treat secondary/endocrine contributors (hypothyroidism, Cushing syndrome) when clinical clues suggest them
Multidisciplinary care with dietitian, exercise specialist and psychologist, treating obesity as a chronic relapsing disease with long-term follow-up
Monitor weight, waist circumference and metabolic parameters over time and reinforce relapse-prevention strategies
